reader.title: Reported lynching of Ben Brand
bases: The later, investigated local report says Brand was publicly whipped and ordered to leave the county and is alive in Sumter county (A6), against earlier reports that he was hanged (A1, A2); the whipping and banishment appear in both Manning Times accounts.

The Manning Times first reported Brand found hanged (A1) and a wire brief said a mob hanged him (A2), but the paper's Bethlehem correspondent later reported after investigating that there was 'no truth whatever' in the hanging and that Brand was alive and picking cotton in Sumter county (A6); this later, specific, local report is the better evidence, so no killing is established. The whipping was done by a 'party' of citizens of unstated size for an alleged insult to a white woman (A6).
A local report (A1) and a wire brief (A2-A5) say Brand was hanged, while a later report in the same local paper denies the hanging and says he was only whipped and banished (A6).

summary.text: The reported lynching of Ben Brand was the reported hanging, in August 1888, of a Black man near Douglass swamp in Salem, South Carolina, after he had been whipped and ordered to leave the county.

The Manning Times and a widely reprinted wire brief said he had been hanged, but the Times later printed its correspondent's report that the hanging never happened and that Brand had only been whipped and banished.
According to the Manning Times, Brand, described as "a negro," went to a white man's house near Salem in early August and obtained permission to spend the night.
The paper said that during the night he "attempted some undue liberties in the house," while its later correspondent described the offense as "grossly insulting a married white woman."
Brand was severely whipped and ordered to leave the county, according to the first report "on penalty of death for failing to do so."
The Times's Bethlehem correspondent wrote that the whipping was done publicly, in the daytime, by "a party of unmasked citizens, white and colored."
On August 29 the Times reported that Brand had not left and had been found dead the previous week, "hanging to a limb of a tree," near Douglass swamp.
No report of an arrest or inquest appears in the coverage.
In a letter dated September 5, the Bethlehem correspondent said he had investigated the reported hanging of "Ben Brand, alias Ben Evans," and found "no truth whatever in it."
He wrote that Brand had left the county and was picking cotton on the Fulwood place in Sumter county.
The Manning Times, published in Clarendon County, carried the first account under the headline "Lynch Law in Salem" and presented the hanging as the consequence of Brand's failure to leave.

In early September a one-sentence brief calling Brand "a desperado who had been detected in a burglary" and saying he was "taken from his captors and hanged by a mob" ran in news-roundup columns of the Narragansett Herald in Rhode Island.
The same brief appeared in the Abbeville Press and Banner, the West Virginia Argus and the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer between September 12 and 14.
On September 19 the Manning Times printed its correspondent's denial under the headline "Was not a Case of Lynching."
No correction of the wire brief was found in the papers that had carried it.

The accounts differ on whether Brand was killed: the first Times report and the wire brief said he was hanged, while the correspondent, writing later after an investigation and naming where Brand was working, said he was alive.
They also differ on the charge, which the local reports gave as an offense in a white household and the wire brief as burglary.
The correspondent described the rumor he denied as a hanging "by Klu Klux," though the first Times report named no perpetrators.

accounts.label: Manning Times first report
accounts.gist: Brand attempted 'undue liberties' in a white man's house, was whipped and ordered to leave on penalty of death, did not leave, and was found hanging from a tree near Douglass swamp.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Brand, 'a desperado' detected in a burglary at Salem, was taken from his captors and hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: Bethlehem correspondent
accounts.gist: The reported hanging 'by Klu Klux' was untrue; Brand was publicly whipped in daytime by unmasked citizens, white and colored, for insulting a married white woman, left the county, and was picking cotton in Sumter county.

framing.detail: The Manning Times reported the hanging under 'Lynch Law in Salem' as the result of Brand's failure to leave ('the result is as above given'), without comment on the mob.
Northern and Southern papers ran a one-sentence brief calling Brand 'a desperado' detected in burglary, in news-roundup columns.
The Manning Times printed its correspondent's denial under 'Was not a Case of Lynching', presenting the whipping as done by 'unmasked citizens, white and colored'.
